topic: I Still Don't Understand Why AI Agents Need Skills

key_points: Original Ask HN post by skeptic_ai questioning why AI agents need skills instead of just well-organized Markdown docs
Core question: 'Couldn't I just have an AGENTS.md that points to folders of .md files?'
Tessl proposes a formal framework for evaluating AI agent skills
Skills as structured, versioned context for coding agents
Focus on reliability and performance evaluation of skills
Claude Skills format has become an open standard for agent skills
Skills use YAML front-matter (name, description) + markdown body for progressive discovery
Non-Claude agents like Codex CLI can adopt the same format with a small enumerator script
Skills directory structure: SKILL.md with front-matter, body loaded only when relevant
Technical report on emerging security threats in the agent skill ecosystem
Skills as an attack vector — malicious skills can compromise agent behavior
Need for security scanning and validation in skill marketplaces
RankClaw audited all 14,706 OpenClaw skills; found 1,103 (7.5%) were malicious
Agent skill ecosystem already large but poorly moderated
Static analysis and AI audit insufficient for catching runtime threats

stats.fact: OpenClaw marketplace had 14,706 skills; 1,103 (7.5%) were found to be malicious
The #1 most downloaded skill on OpenClaw marketplace was malware
Claude Code skills format uses YAML front-matter (name, description, allowed-tools) + markdown body for progressive disclosure
Skills are lazy-loaded: only name and description are shown to the LLM initially; full body is loaded only when the agent decides the skill is relevant
stats.source: HN discussion — nijave, bad_username, watchdog408 comments

stats.fact: Context window pollution is the key architectural reason for skills: loading all instructions into context degrades LLM performance
Skills can bundle deterministic scripts and artifacts (not just markdown), enabling executable behavior beyond prompting

angles: Skills are just lazy-loaded Markdown — the 'lazy' part is the entire point, not a bug
Context window management: why dumping everything into AGENTS.md hurts performance
The security nightmare: 7.5% of skills in the largest marketplace were malicious
Skills as an open standard: Claude Code format adopted by Codex CLI and others
Beyond prompting: skills that bundle executable scripts and artifacts
The npm-for-AI-skills vision: community registries, versioning, and trust
Progressive disclosure as a design pattern for agent instructions
Skeptic's guide: what you're NOT missing (skills really are just organized docs with a loading mechanism)
outline: H2: The Question That Started It All — the Ask HN post and the core confusion
H2: What Are Skills, Really? — skills as lazy-loaded, progressively-disclosed Markdown with front-matter
H2: Why Not Just AGENTS.md? — context pollution, performance, and the limits of dumping everything into context
H2: The Open Standard — how Claude Code's skill format became cross-platform (Codex CLI, etc.)
H2: Beyond Markdown — skills that bundle scripts, artifacts, and executable behavior
H2: The Security Reality Check — 7.5% of OpenClaw skills were malicious; the #1 download was malware
H2: The npm-for-Skills Vision — community registries, versioning, trust, and the Generalized approach
H2: What the Skeptic Was Right About — skills really are just organized docs with a smarter loading mechanism
H2: What the Skeptic Was Missing — the architectural benefits of progressive disclosure, composability, and context management
H2: The Bottom Line — skills are a packaging convention, not magic, and that's exactly what makes them useful
